sections.h2: Offices that value and bill Montgomery County property
sections.html:
Both offices operate from one address, 350 Pageant Lane in Clarksville. The Assessor of Property works from Suite 101-C and puts a value on every parcel. The County Trustee sits in Suite 101-B and sends the bills.

  • Assessor of Property: 931-648-5709, counter open 8 to 4:30 on weekdays.
  • County Trustee: 931-648-5717, open weekdays from half past seven until 4:30.
  • Delinquent tax suits: the Clerk and Master of the Montgomery Chancery Court, 2 Millennium Plaza, Suite 101, 931-648-5703.

Commissioners adopt the rate each year, and the Trustee applies it to every $100 of assessed value. A house inside Clarksville limits also receives a bill from the City of Clarksville, so a seller there has two balances to clear.

Clarksville is the county seat and the only incorporated municipality in Montgomery County, which belongs to the Clarksville, TN-KY metro area. The Census estimate for July 2025 is 249,935 residents, up 13.6% from 220,012 at the 2020 base. The county has 102,547 housing units, and owners live in 61.9% of homes. A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $280,200, median household income is $75,613 and median gross rent is $1,308.

Because most homes here are owned rather than rented, a seller is usually dealing with a single owner-occupied bill, plus a city bill if the house is inside Clarksville. Before you pick a list price, learn which of those two bills applies to your address and whether either one has money still owed on it. A quick call to the Trustee at 931-648-5717 answers the county half, and the city Finance and Revenue Department answers the rest.

sections.h2: 2026 tax rates and how a bill is figured
sections.html:
The county rate for 2026 is $2.10 per $100 of assessed value, and Clarksville's rate is $1.01. A property inside the city therefore carries a combined $3.11 per $100, while a house outside the city pays the county rate alone.

How a parcel is used decides what share of its appraisal gets taxed. The Trustee's method is to multiply the appraisal by the class percentage, divide by 100, then multiply by the rate.

Assessment percentage by property class
Property classShare of appraised value assessed
Residential and farm25%
Personal property30%
Commercial and industrial40%
Public utilities55%

The sums come out differently for every parcel, so check this arithmetic against the notice mailed to you. Anything that changes the class of your land, such as farm use, or an approved relief program, moves the final figure.

sections.h2: When is the bill due, and what does paying late cost?
sections.html:
Bills go out by mail in the last week of October. Payment opens the first Monday in October and closes on the last day of February with no interest. From March 1, each month adds 1.5 percent to the base tax, which works out to 18 percent a year.

State law does not oblige the Trustee to mail notices, and the county will not excuse lateness because a bill went missing. If you have not received one by early November, call and ask. Partial payments toward the current year can start July 10, provided the balance is cleared by the February cutoff. A payment sent through the Postal Service counts on its postmark date, but an office meter stamp does not.

Online e-checks carry a 1.75 percent plus $1 charge, and Visa or MasterCard payments carry 2.65 percent plus $1. Only the counter takes cash. A handful of neighborhood banks take current-year payments until February 28, as long as you carry the original bill or a printout from the Trustee's website.

City tax has its own ladder. Once an account is twelve months behind, Clarksville refers it to a delinquent tax attorney, and any later payment is made to the Clerk and Master at the chancery court.

sections.h2: How to contest a Montgomery County valuation
sections.html:
Begin by calling the Assessor, 931-648-5709. A miscounted room or wrong land class is frequently fixed on that one call. Disputes that survive go to the county equalization board, which starts its session on the first business day of June and keeps meeting until its docket is done.

Hearing slots are booked through the Assessor, and the phone window runs from May 15 to May 31. The board has five property owners from around the county, and state law reserves two seats for Clarksville residents. You can appear yourself or send a relative, lawyer or authorized agent. Bring appraisals, repair bills and comparable assessments, and skip arguments about what you can afford, since the board weighs value only.

You should get the board's decision letter ahead of July. If you still disagree, the State Board of Equalization takes the next appeal, which must reach it by August 1 or 45 days after the county mailing, whichever falls later. The countywide reappraisal is next due in 2029.

sections.h2: Tax relief and special bills that affect a sale
sections.html:
Tennessee's relief program refunds part of the tax for low-income elderly owners, disabled owners, and disabled veteran owners with their surviving spouses. It works as a reimbursement, so you still receive the bill and pay it. Only the home you live in qualifies, and a house held in an irrevocable trust is left out.

In Clarksville, the Trustee's office is where you sign up for the Tax Freeze program. Relief applications are available at both the county Trustee and the city Finance and Revenue Department. Approved owners get a voucher with each bill and must send it in every year to both offices.

Greenbelt land brings another charge. If a sale ends the farm, forest or open-space classification, rollback taxes for the previous three years (five for open space) come due, and unless the contract says otherwise the seller owes them. A buyer who promises to keep the classification has 90 days after the sale to file the form with the Assessor, or the rollback becomes the buyer's problem. Whichever side owes it, an unpaid rollback attaches to the land as a first lien.

sections.h2: How does the tax get settled at closing?
sections.html:
New owners are told to check the closing statement or ask the title company about the year's tax. Whatever the purchase contract says, unpaid tax keeps building on the house itself, and a delinquent Clarksville property can still be sent to a tax auction.

  1. Request a balance from the Trustee for county tax and from city Finance and Revenue for city tax.
  2. Find out whether your lender already paid from escrow, because the city refunds a double payment to whoever paid last.
  3. Give the title company both figures so it can pay any remaining balance out of your proceeds.
  4. Check that the closing statement shows the county and city lines separately for a Clarksville address.

If a payoff looks larger than expected, ask the office for a year-by-year breakdown ahead of closing day instead of at the table. Buyers who pay cash and take the house as-is still want those same payoffs, and having them in hand early lets the closing date stay put.

faqs.q: What are the 2026 property tax rates in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: The county charges $2.10 per $100 of assessed value, and Clarksville charges $1.01 on top of that inside city limits. A residential parcel is assessed at 25 percent of its appraised value.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to pay Montgomery County tax without interest?
faqs.a: The last day of February. The window opens on the first Monday of October, and from March 1 interest of 1.5 percent a month is added to the base tax.

faqs.q: Where do I start if my Montgomery County valuation looks too high?
faqs.a: Call the Assessor at 931-648-5709. If that fails, book a June hearing with the County Board of Equalization by calling between May 15 and May 31, and use the State Board of Equalization after that.

faqs.q: Does a Clarksville house owe both city and county tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The Trustee collects only the county share, and the city bills its own. Homes outside the city limits owe the county portion alone.

faqs.q: Who owes the tax when a Montgomery County house sells?
faqs.a: The sale contract and closing statement settle the split between buyer and seller. The tax follows the calendar year and the property itself, so the title company should confirm the split and clear any balance at closing.
